title: Design Splitwise
summary: An expense splitter is a ledger with a settlement algorithm bolted on. Most candidates get the classes right and then quietly produce a system that loses a cent per transaction — and the interviewer is watching for exactly that.

blocks.title: What you are actually being asked
blocks.text: Two things, and only two. **Can you model money without losing money** — which rules out floats and forces you to decide who absorbs a rounding remainder. And **can you settle a debt graph** — reducing *n* people owing each other into the fewest transfers. The class diagram is the easy half.

Users belong to groups. Any user can add an expense they paid for, split among some subset of users — equally, by exact amounts, or by percentage. The system tracks who owes whom, and can settle a group with as few payments as possible.

items.title: Equal, exact, percentage — all three?
items.text: They are three implementations of one interface. Confirm which are in scope, then build the interface anyway.

items.title: Multiple currencies?
items.text: If yes, an amount without a currency is meaningless and every balance needs one. Usually out of scope; ask so you can say you asked.

items.title: Can an expense be edited or deleted after the fact?
items.text: This decides whether balances are stored or derived. It is the biggest architectural fork in the question.

items.title: Simplify debts automatically, or on demand?
items.text: Splitwise itself makes this a setting, because automatic simplification confuses people who wanted to pay a specific person.

items.title: Who absorbs the rounding remainder?
items.text: Splitting £10 three ways is 3.33, 3.33, 3.34. Someone pays the extra penny. Ask who — it signals that you know money is not divisible.

blocks.title: Never use floating point for money
blocks.text: `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3`. Use integer minor units — pennies, cents — or `BigDecimal` with an explicit rounding mode. A candidate who writes `double amount` has told the interviewer they have never shipped anything financial, whatever else they say afterwards.

blocks.title: Ledger first, balances derived
blocks.caption: `ExpenseBook` is the source of truth. Balances are a projection of it — which is what makes editing and deleting an expense a solved problem rather than a data-repair exercise.
blocks.code:
classDiagram
    class ExpenseBook {
        -List~Expense~ expenses
        +void add(Expense e)
        +void remove(String expenseId)
        +Map~Pair, Money~ balances()
        +List~Transfer~ settle(SettlementStrategy s)
    }
    class Expense {
        -String id
        -User paidBy
        -Money amount
        -SplitStrategy split
        -List~User~ participants
        +Map~User, Money~ shares()
    }
    class SplitStrategy {
        <<interface>>
        +Map~User, Money~ divide(Money total, List~User~ users)
    }
    class Money {
        -long minorUnits
        -Currency currency
        +Money plus(Money o)
        +List~Money~ allocate(int ways)
    }
    ExpenseBook o-- Expense
    Expense --> SplitStrategy
    Expense --> Money
    SplitStrategy <|.. EqualSplit
    SplitStrategy <|.. ExactSplit
    SplitStrategy <|.. PercentSplit

blocks.title: Store the ledger, derive the balances
blocks.text: *“I would keep expenses as the source of truth and derive balances, because deleting an expense then becomes removing a row rather than reverse-engineering which balances it touched.”* If you store balances directly, every edit is a migration and every bug is permanent.

blocks.title: Say the invariant out loud
blocks.text: *“The sum of the parts equals the whole, always — that is what `allocate` guarantees and what naive division does not.”* Then mention the fairness wrinkle: allocating the remainder from the front means the same person always pays the extra penny, so real systems rotate it.
Six friends, twenty expenses, everyone owes everyone. Settling naively is up to *n²* transfers. The question is how few you can do.

blocks.title: From a tangle to a minimum set of transfers
blocks.caption: Collapse the graph to one net balance per person, then repeatedly match the largest debtor with the largest creditor. Any group of *n* people settles in at most *n − 1* transfers.
blocks.code:
flowchart LR subgraph R["Raw debts"] A1["A owes B 10"]; B1["B owes C 10"]; C1["A owes C 5"] end subgraph N["Net balances"] A2["A: −15"]; B2["B: 0"]; C2["C: +15"] end subgraph S["Settlement"] T["A pays C 15
1 transfer, not 3"] end R --> N --> S

blocks.title: Greedy is not provably minimal
blocks.text: Minimising transfers exactly is NP-hard — it reduces to a subset-sum-style partition problem. Greedy gives at most *n − 1*, which is good and usually optimal in practice. **Say this.** Claiming greedy is optimal is a wrong answer confidently delivered; naming the bound and the hardness is a right one.

blocks.caption: `n` people, `m` expenses.
rows: O(m × k) — a fold over the ledger
O(n log n) — heap operations over net balances

items.title: Multiple currencies
items.text: `Money` already carries one, so addition across currencies must fail rather than coerce. Conversion needs a rate *and a timestamp* — a balance converted at today's rate silently rewrites history.

items.title: Edit or delete an expense
items.text: Free, because balances are derived. This is the payoff for the ledger decision and worth pointing at explicitly.

items.title: Partial settlement
items.text: A payment is just another ledger entry with a `SETTLEMENT` type. Do not special-case it into the balance code.

items.title: Do not simplify across people who do not know each other
items.text: Real Splitwise constrains simplification to a group. Netting A→B→C into A→C is mathematically fine and socially strange.

items.title: Show a running activity feed
items.text: The ledger is already an event log, so the feed is a projection of it. Another payoff for storing expenses rather than balances.

items.title: Scale it
items.text: The HLD pivot: the ledger is append-only and shards by group, balances become a materialised view, and settlement runs on demand rather than on write.

blocks.text: Edge cases to state before you are asked

items: An expense where the payer is not a participant — legal: they paid, they owe nothing, everyone else owes them.
Exact split whose shares do not sum to the total → reject loudly at construction.
Percentage split not summing to 100 → same.
Splitting an amount among more people than there are minor units — £0.02 three ways gives [1, 1, 0]. Someone gets nothing, and the total still balances.
A user in a group with zero net balance must not appear in the settlement at all.
Self-transfer: a user paying themselves is a no-op, not a ledger entry.

rows: Integer minor units, or `BigDecimal` with a rounding mode
`allocate` preserves the total; mentions rotating who absorbs it
Stores the ledger and derives balances
Net out, then greedy match, ≤ n − 1
Names the n − 1 bound and that exact minimisation is NP-hard

blocks.title: The 45-minute plan
blocks.text: **0–6** clarify split types, currency, edits, and who eats the rounding. **6–10** say “integer minor units” and draw the ledger. **10–20** classes plus `SplitStrategy`. **20–30** code `allocate` and `EqualSplit` — the money invariant is the highest-value code you will write. **30–40** settlement with the heap, and the NP-hard caveat. **40–45** edits, or multi-currency.
